You are considering a bet of 10. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. For this comparison only, assume Candidate 1 calls, Candidate 2 folds and Candidate 3 calls. These stipulated responses exclude raises.
cases.prompt: Compare every candidate with your best five. What does Candidate 2's fold change relative to checking, and is it a fold by a hand that beats you? Does Candidate 3's call supply value from a worse hand? What is needed to compare the bet with checking overall?
points: Your best five are the board's ten-high straight. Candidate 1 makes a queen-high straight and beats you. Candidates 2 and 3 both play the ten-high board straight and tie you.

Candidate 2's fold wins the existing pot instead of splitting it, but does not make a stronger hand fold. Candidate 3's tied call supplies no value from a worse hand; equal new contributions are split back under these no-fee assumptions.

Candidate 1's call loses the ten-counter bet. The comparison must weigh that cost against the benefit of tied hands folding and any other responses. These example rows do not establish the needed frequencies.
cases.misconception: Treating every fold as a stronger-hand fold or every call as value, even when the board creates ties.
cases.focus: folding-a-tied-hand
cases.design_note: This case distinguishes a tied fold that gains an otherwise shared pot from a tied call and a losing call against an improved straight.

cases.title: Three holdings and a proposed bet
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 32 counters and both players have 80 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 8. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. Consider the three candidate holdings. Their responses to the proposed bet have not been assigned.
cases.prompt: Compare all three candidates with your best five. Which could support a value-bet explanation if they called, and what must you learn about their responses? Does beating two listed holdings establish that betting earns more than checking?
points: Your A-A-T-9-7 beats Candidate 1's A-A-T-8-7 and Candidate 3's A-Q-J-T-7. It loses to Candidate 2's T-T-T-A-7.

Candidates 1 and 3 could be value targets if they call the proposed amount. Being weaker does not supply that call assumption; their responses, including folds or raises where allowed, must be modeled or supported.

Beating two listed hands does not establish a better bet. Checking already wins against those hands, and the comparison needs their frequencies and their responses to this amount, as well as the cost of responses from hands that beat you.
cases.misconception: Inferring that a physically weaker holding will call even though no response assumption was supplied.
cases.focus: holding-strength-without-response-data
cases.design_note: This case deliberately leaves every response unspecified so the learner must distinguish conditional value targets from assumed callers.

cases.title: A revised river bet amount
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 36 counters and both players have 100 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 12. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. An earlier study note about a bet of 4 assumed Candidate 1 would call. For the current bet of 12 only, assume Candidates 1 and 3 fold and Candidate 2 calls. These current responses exclude raises.
cases.prompt: Compare all three candidates with your final hand. Does increasing the bet from 4 to 12 triple the value obtained from Candidate 1 under the stated change? What happens on the current call, and what further information is needed before comparing this bet with checking across the full decision?
points: Your K-K-J-8-6 beats Candidate 1's K-K-T-8-6 and Candidate 3's A-K-Q-8-6. Candidate 2 has 8-8-8-K-6 and beats you.
Candidate 1 now folds, so it contributes no new counters to the larger bet. Tripling a bet does not triple payment from a hand whose assumed response changes from calling to folding.

The current call from Candidate 2 loses twelve new counters, while checking would already win against Candidates 1 and 3. Comparing the current bet with checking requires the full set of possible holdings, their frequencies and their responses to the twelve-counter bet; these examples alone do not establish that it improves on checking.
cases.misconception: Scaling value with bet size while ignoring a changed caller response.
cases.focus: response-changes-with-bet-size
cases.design_note: This case changes the stated response of one candidate when the amount increases, so the learner must not preserve a smaller-bet caller assumption.

cases.title: A call followed by a reveal
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 28 counters and both players have 70 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 7. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. For this comparison only, assume each listed candidate calls the proposed bet, with no raises.
cases.prompt: Compare all three candidates with your best five and identify any value targets. Suppose Candidate 2 is revealed after the bet is called: does that result alone disprove a value-bet purpose? What is needed to assess the earlier bet against checking?
points: Your K-K-T-9-6 beats Candidate 1's K-K-9-8-6 and Candidate 3's Q-Q-K-9-6. Both are assumed to call and are possible value targets.
Candidate 2 has 9-9-9-K-6 and beats you, so its call loses the new bet. That single result does not erase the possible weaker callers or by itself disprove a value-bet intention.

The earlier comparison with checking depends on the possible holdings, responses and frequencies at that decision. A losing result does not establish a bad bet, just as naming weaker callers does not establish a profitable one.
cases.misconception: Judging the validity of a value-bet explanation solely from one losing showdown.
cases.focus: losing-result-and-value-intention
cases.design_note: This case reveals a losing caller after a proposed value bet and asks the learner to retain the distinction between intention, expected comparison and one result.

cases.title: A pair of twos and three responses
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 32 counters and both players have 80 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 8. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. For this comparison only, assume Candidate 1 folds, Candidate 2 calls and Candidate 3 folds. These stipulated responses exclude raises.
cases.prompt: Compare all three candidates with your best five. Which fold could support a bluff explanation, and does having a made pair prevent that purpose? What does the other fold establish, and what is missing from a comparison with checking?
points: Your 2-2-A-K-Q loses to Candidate 1's J-J-A-K-Q and Candidate 2's A-A-K-Q-9. It beats Candidate 3's A-K-Q-9-7.
Candidate 1's assumed fold supports a bluff explanation because its jacks beat your twos. A bet can aim to fold a better hand even when the betting hand is a made pair.

Candidate 3 folds a hand you would beat by checking, while Candidate 2 calls and costs your new eight counters. An overall comparison needs the frequencies of these and other possible holdings and responses; one fold or a made pair does not establish the preferred action.
cases.misconception: Assuming that every bet with a made pair must be for value, or that every fold shows a successful stronger-hand bluff.
cases.focus: made-pair-used-as-a-bluff
cases.design_note: This case uses a small made pair as a possible bluffing hand, with one stronger fold, one weaker fold and one losing call.

cases.title: Two private hearts on the final board
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 28 counters and both players have 70 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 7. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. For this comparison only, assume Candidate 1 folds, Candidate 2 folds and Candidate 3 calls. These stipulated responses exclude raises.
cases.prompt: What hand do you actually have now, and can a later shared card still complete a flush? Compare all candidates and identify which fold could support a bluff explanation. What does checking retain against Candidate 2, and what else is needed to compare the bet overall?
points: You have A-K-J-8-6, an ace-high hand, not a flush. There are only four hearts among your seven cards and no further community card after the river.
Candidate 1 has Q-Q-K-8-6 and beats you, so its assumed fold supports a bluff explanation. Candidate 2 has A-K-9-8-6 and loses to your jack kicker. Candidate 3 has 8-8-8-K-6 and beats you.

Checking would still win against Candidate 2; its fold is not a stronger-hand fold. Candidate 3's call loses the new seven counters. The full comparison needs the frequencies of the possible holdings and responses, including the showdown value retained by checking.
cases.misconception: Treating a missed river draw as having no possible showdown value or as still having a card to come.
cases.focus: missed-draw-with-showdown-value
cases.design_note: This case requires recognizing a missed flush draw while preserving an ace-high kicker win that matters when comparing betting with checking.

cases.title: Two private ranks on a paired river
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 36 counters and both players have 90 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 9. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. For this comparison only, assume Candidate 1 folds, Candidate 2 calls and Candidate 3 folds. These stipulated responses exclude raises.
cases.prompt: Choose your best five and compare each candidate, explaining the kicker where it matters. Which response supports a bluff explanation even though you can name two pairs? Which other outcomes must you include before comparing betting with checking?
points: Your best five are K-K-8-8-7. Candidate 1 has K-K-A-Q-8 and loses. Candidate 2 has K-K-K-8-7 and wins. Candidate 3 has K-K-8-8-A and wins on the ace kicker; your second private rank does not add a third pair to the best five.
Candidate 3's assumed fold is a fold by a better two-pair hand, so it can support a bluff explanation. Calling your own hand two pair does not determine the bet's purpose.

Candidate 1's fold adds no new opposing counters and checking would already beat it. Candidate 2's call loses nine new counters. Compare those possibilities and the stronger fold using a full response model and frequencies before claiming betting improves on checking.
cases.misconception: Using the two-pair label to skip kicker comparisons or to label every bet as value.
cases.focus: counterfeited-two-pair-and-purpose
cases.design_note: This case makes a same-two-pair kicker loss the bluff target while a different candidate loses to checking and a third wins when calling.

cases.title: A call with two listed explanations
cases.setup: In this fictional heads-up river exercise, the pot is 24 counters and both players have 60 behind. The opponent checks to you last to act. Checking is legal and would end betting. You are considering a bet of 6. No money is wagered; no fees, side pots or tournament prizes are modeled. For this comparison only, assume Candidates 1 and 2 call and Candidate 3 folds. These stipulated responses exclude raises.
cases.prompt: Compare each candidate with your best five. If you bet and get called, does that action identify one exact holding or tell you whether you are ahead? Replace the reason "to find out where I am" with a specific target and state what remains unknown when comparing the bet with checking.
points: Your J-J-T-T-9 beats Candidate 1's J-J-9-9-T and Candidate 3's A-K-J-T-9. Candidate 2 makes a jack-high straight, J-T-9-8-7, and beats you.
Both Candidate 1 and Candidate 2 call under the stated assumptions, yet one loses to you and one wins. The call therefore does not identify an exact hand or settle whether you are ahead.

A testable value intention is to get Candidate 1's worse two pair to call six counters. Candidate 2's call would beat you and must also be counted, and Candidate 3 folds a hand checking would beat. Their frequencies and any other possible responses remain necessary for comparing the bet with checking.
cases.misconception: Betting for information as though one observed call reveals a unique hand or guarantees that the caller is weaker.
cases.focus: call-does-not-identify-one-hand
cases.design_note: This case gives the same observed calling action to holdings on opposite sides of the showdown comparison, requiring an explicit value target instead of an information-only reason.
